1:
A new governor changes nothing. Henry opens on that: new lords, new laws, new customs, we say; but Paul had the same treatment from Festus as from Felix — not so just as he should have been, for he does not release him, and not so unjust as the Jews wished, for he will not condemn him. Calvin gives the reason for the danger: new rulers, to win the favour of the provinces, grant them many things at their first coming, so Paul’s death would have been a fine means for Festus to win favour.

Their speed is what strikes them. Henry counts the days: Festus stayed three days at Caesarea, where Paul was a prisoner, and Paul made no application to him; but the moment he comes up to Jerusalem the priests are in all haste. See how restless a thing malice is — Paul more patiently bears the lengthening of his imprisonment than his enemies do the delay of his prosecution. Robertson quotes another hand: this renewal of the charge after two years, on the very first opportunity, measures not only their unsleeping hatred but the importance they attached to Paul’s influence. Wesley puts it in a line — in so long a time their rage was not cooled, so much louder a call had Paul to the Gentiles.

Who applied is disputed: Gill and Ellicott both report that the better copies read ‘the chief priests’, the whole college. Barnes tries to name him: the high priest at this time was Ismael the son of Fabi, though he thinks Ananias is meant, since a deposed high priest kept the title. Ellicott reads their timing as calculation: they hoped to profit by the newness of Festus to his office, thinking he would yield to men powerful enough to procure his predecessor’s recall.

The request was specious and the design was murder. Henry sets out both: it looked reasonable that a man charged with profaning the temple be tried where the fact was committed, but what they designed was to way-lay him on the road, supposing he would not be brought under so strong a guard as he was sent down with. He fastens on the word: they desired favour against Paul, when the favour ought to be for the prisoner. Ellicott is blunter: once again priests and scribes are ready for the weapon of the assassin.

Why Festus refused divides them cleanly. Barnes offers a legal reason: he was probably apprized that Paul was a Roman citizen, whose case could not come before the council but must be heard by the governor. Robertson makes it jurisdiction and suspicion: Festus was wholly within his rights to insist they bring their charges to Caesarea. Clarke calls it truly astonishing that Festus should refuse a favour which to those not in the secret must appear so reasonable, and answers that God had told Paul he should testify at Rome and disposed the governor’s heart. Wesley agrees: his care to preserve the imperial privileges was the means of preserving Paul’s life — by what invisible springs does God govern the world! Calvin says it in his own idiom: God held the governor’s mind with the secret bridle of his providence, so that he stoutly denied what he was afterward ready to grant.

The last phrase divides them again. Gill and Wesley take ‘those among you which are able’ practically: who are at leisure, who can bear the expense, whose health and age admit it, and who are masters of the affair. Calvin agrees and supplies the back-story: they had objected the trouble and charges, and begged that their chief men, some very aged, not be wearied with a superfluous journey. Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson read it as power rather than capacity: men in office whose character is a pledge for their depositions, the leaders of the people and not a hired rhetorician.
6:
The first clause is a textual problem, and four of them stop for it. Clarke says the strangeness of the expression suggests the printed text is not quite correct, and reports that the best manuscripts read ‘not more than eight or ten days’ — a reading one editor admitted into his text and a scholar of the day pronounced doubtless genuine. Barnes lists the same witnesses. Gill notes that some versions drop the negative altogether, and explains that the historian was not certain to a day and so expresses himself loosely. Wesley finds the shorter reading fitting on its own account: a short space for a new governor to stay at such a city, and too short to have heard and decided Paul’s cause.

The court is set with deliberate form. Robertson observes that Festus lost no time, the chief men having come down with him, and that sitting on the judgment seat was a legal formality to give weight to the decision. He notices what the accusers do with their bodies: they took their stand around him, and having no advocate this time they mass their forces to impress the governor, bearing down with many and grievous charges.

What the charges were has to be reconstructed from the reply. Clarke reads them as three — the law broken, the temple defiled, treasonable practices — and supposes the political counts were invented, since the accusers must have perceived the governor would not intermeddle with questions of their law. Ellicott gives the same three in fuller dress: he had broken the law of Israel, which Rome recognised as the religion of the province; he had profaned the temple; and he taught that there was another king than Nero. Robertson agrees the last was the one to interest Festus, and if proved would make Paul guilty of treason; he adds that the denial is complete and no proof was offered, repetition and vehemence taking its place. Wesley compresses the whole into an aphorism: when many accusations are heaped together, frequently not one of them is true.

Calvin will not leave it at the trial. So long as Paul lived under the law his integrity was famous, and converted he was a singular pattern of innocence; yet he is subject to slanders, and this is almost always the estate of the servants of Christ, who must be the more courageous to pass through evil report and good report. The wicked can never be so bridled that they will not speak evil of good men, therefore the command to stop their mouths cannot mean that the upright escape backbiting, but that our life may answer for us and wipe away the blots of false infamy.

On the proposal they agree about the motive and divide about the risk. Barnes says he showed a desire of popularity rather than an inclination to do justice, since had he meant to do right he would have discharged Paul at once; Gill notes he had just entered his government and met with civilities from the Jews; Clarke adds that he knew Paul was a Roman citizen and could not be obliged to a new trial at Jerusalem. Robertson is harshest: Festus had no more courage to do right than Felix, and if he would not give Paul justice at Caesarea, where his own court sat, what assurance was there that he would give it in the atmosphere of Jerusalem? Ellicott is the one dissenter, finding the invitation plausible in itself, since it offered a trial before the national tribunal with the governor present as a check on violence. Calvin wonders why Festus gave Paul a choice rather than simply ordering him up, and answers that he feared to infringe the privilege of a Roman citizen; Wesley says only that God secretly overruled the whole, that Paul might have occasion to appeal to Rome.
10:
The claim rests on where he is standing. Gill denies the legend that a seat had been built in the hall for the emperor should he ever come: it is Caesar’s seat because the court is Roman and Festus who fills it represents Caesar. Clarke and Wesley say the same — every procurator represented the person of the emperor, and every court was held in his name. Robertson catches the tense, a periphrastic perfect, and presses the consequence: Festus had no right to hand a Roman citizen to a Jewish tribunal, which he half admitted by asking whether Paul was willing. Ellicott hears the same continuous force, and rejects a rival reading of the words — the paraphrase that Paul already stood in purpose before the emperor’s court because God had revealed he must preach at Rome. Robertson renders the reproach that follows as a comparative, as thou dost understand better than thou art willing to admit, and says Paul exposes the governor with merciless precision; Clarke supplies the paperwork, since the record of the trial before Felix must have passed to his successor with the prisoner.

The offer to die is taken as proof of the appeal’s honesty. Barnes makes the rule: no true Christian wishes to escape the laws, but he has rights like other men, and boldness is not incompatible with Christianity — innocence, when its rights are invaded, is always bold. Calvin turns it into a permission: having professed that he does not refuse to die if guilty, Paul freely uses such helps as he could find at the hands of men, and if we are brought into like straits we must not be superstitious but may crave the help of the laws, since magistrates are appointed by God.

Clarke finds the sharpest thing here in a word repeated three times. The Jews asked a favour of Festus; Festus, willing to do them that favour, put the question to Paul; Paul answers that no man can make a present of him to them; and Festus afterwards uses the same verb to Agrippa. Ellicott renders it as bluntly — no man may give me up to them as a favour — which shows Paul saw through the simulated fairness of the procurator. Robertson adds that the ‘may’ is legal: not even Festus can make a free gift of a Roman citizen.

On the appeal itself they turn historian. Barnes names the old statutes under which a citizen threatened with scourging or death could appeal to the Roman people, and notes that under the emperors it was carried to the emperor instead. Ellicott makes it an essay in constitutional decline: consuls were still elected and went through the shadowy functions of their office, but the emperor had gathered every balancing power into himself, and the tribunes’ protective office became by a subtle artifice the instrument of a centralised tyranny. Clarke notes the appeal lay even before sentence if the judge acted against law. Calvin guards it theologically: Paul does not make the gospel subject to a profane man’s judgment, but appeals from a court where he could no longer hope for equity.

Whether the reply is relief or a sneer they cannot settle. Clarke infers from the conference that the appeal was conditional, since Festus could not otherwise have deliberated whether to grant what he had no power to refuse; Robertson says instead that some discretion was allowed, an appeal being refusable for a notorious robber or pirate. Barnes and Clarke read the answer as escape: Festus got his hand creditably drawn out of a trial he could not decide without offending someone. Ellicott hears a sneer — Festus knew better than the apostle what kind of judge he was appealing to, and how long the delays would be. Calvin suspects indignation, then withdraws, leaving it indifferent because it leans only on conjecture.
13:
Henry makes something of the visit itself. Kings usually think it enough to send their ambassadors to congratulate their friends, but here was a king who came himself, and made the majesty of a prince yield to the satisfaction of a friend, since personal converse is the pleasantest thing among friends. He suspects they came as much to divert themselves and to show their fine clothes, which would do vain people no good if they did not go abroad.

On who Agrippa was they compete in detail. Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson rehearse the same career from the historian: son of the Herod who killed James and was eaten of worms, too young at his father’s death to be given Judea, made king of Chalcis by Claudius, given the tetrarchies of Philip and Lysanias, and enlarged again by Nero. Clarke and Ellicott add what most concerned the Jews, that he held the superintendence of the temple and the nomination of the high priests; Robertson says he angered them by building his palace to overlook the temple and by frequent changes in that office, and calls him the last Jewish king in Palestine. Henry alone reports a rabbinic story: reading the law publicly and coming to the words ‘thou shalt not set a stranger king over thee’, the tears ran down his cheeks, for he was not of the seed of Israel; and the congregation cried out, be of good comfort, king Agrippa, thou art our brother.

On Bernice they are unanimous and unsparing. Wesley calls it a scandalous familiarity; Clarke says she was violently suspected of an incestuous life and quotes a satirist on the famous diamond given to an incestuous sister; Ellicott says her history reads like a horrible romance. Calvin is the most careful: the historians nowhere say she was her brother’s wife, and one assigns her a dominion of her own, so it is to be thought that, hardened in their wickedness, they dwelt together without regarding what men said, yet abstained from marriage lest it betray and augment their crime. Robertson notes she left the king of Cilicia she had married, and later became the mistress of Titus. Henry draws the moral: such lewd people were the great people generally in those times — say not that the former days were better.

Why the case came up is variously guessed. Gill supposes idleness: they had been there many days indulging themselves and conversing on various subjects, and the matter served to pass the time. Calvin says it more sharply — when they wanted matter of talk, as idle men use to invent somewhat whereon they may talk, mention was made of Paul. Ellicott thinks it came in in the course of conversation, Festus supposing that a man who knew all about the Jews could throw light on a prisoner denounced by his own compatriots though professing the utmost reverence for the law and the temple. Clarke and Barnes make it consultation: Festus knew Agrippa was better acquainted with such matters, and wished to make him a party to the business.

Two will not let ‘left in bonds’ pass quietly. Robertson takes it as a perfect participle meaning left behind, and turns it into an indictment: Paul is one of the leavings of Felix, a sort of junk left on his hands, and this cowardly procurator so pictures the greatest of living men and the greatest preacher of all time to a profligate pair of sinners. Calvin observes that Festus, making a show of wonderful equity, condemns himself unawares by confessing Paul was forced to appeal to avoid being carried to Jerusalem; and he gives the point of the long narration — that though the cause was broken off, Paul’s bands were famous, and he had more liberty to preach the gospel in prison than if he had lived free in a private house.
15:
What the Jews asked is sharper in the Greek than in the English. Clarke reports that the best manuscripts read not judgment but condemnation, a sentence of death, and thinks the harder word genuine: nothing could satisfy these men but the death of the apostle — it was not justice they wanted but his destruction. Robertson notes the word is the only instance of it in the New Testament, an old term for penalty compounded of the words for against and justice. Wesley catches the presumption: they asked judgment as upon a previous conviction, which they falsely pretended. Barnes glosses it plainly — they would have him condemned.

The rule Festus cites draws the strangest agreement in the chapter: Barnes and Clarke both turn it into a tribute to their own country’s courts. Both first pile up the ancient authorities: the historian who says it is not their custom to condemn men before they are heard, the Jewish writer who describes judges hearing both sides impartially, deciding neither from enmity nor favour. Then each goes home. Barnes calls it a subject of sincere gratitude to the God of his nation that the privilege is enjoyed there in the highest perfection, their jurisprudence surpassing all that Rome ever enjoyed. Clarke says England can boast such laws not in her statute books only but in constant operation, that not even the king could imprison a man without the regular procedure of law, and that in this favoured country there are no arbitrary imprisonments, no Bastiles, no lettres de cachet: the law makes the king. Wesley states the principle bare: how excellent a rule, to condemn no one unheard, and one that ought to direct our proceedings in private life as well as public.

The tone they hear differently from the substance. Ellicott finds a certain ostentation in the way Festus speaks of the manner of the Romans, announcing as with a flourish of trumpets that he at least means to be rigidly impartial — though he adds that so far as we know the conduct matched the profession. He catches something else: Festus uses the very verb Paul had used about being given up as a favour, which shows the arrow shot at a venture had hit the mark, and that Festus is eager to repel the charge. Robertson hears a touch of disdain and a tone of scorn towards the Jews; he notes that the optative in the clause about hearing the accused is literary Greek found nowhere else in the New Testament, and concedes that the speech, as a speech, all sounds fair enough.

The surprise is the last thing Festus reports, and they explain it by what he had expected. Barnes says it was natural to suppose they would accuse Paul of a breach of the peace or some atrocious crime, given two years in custody and the violence of the Jews. Clarke assembles the record as a new governor would have seen it — twice snatched from the hands of the Jews, brought a prisoner to Caesarea, tried before the council and the governor, two years in bonds, the high priest and all the heads of the nation demanding his condemnation — and asks how surprised he must have been to find scarcely anything amounting to a crime laid to his charge. Wesley puts the cause in three words: from their passion and vehemence. Robertson finds it in the tense, an imperfect fixing the governor’s state of mind before the trial; Gill notes only that the accusers had to stand up while producing their proofs.

Calvin marvels at the admission. Paul had been accused of sedition, and yet Festus says nothing was charged of the kind he expected; from which we may plainly know that their accusations were so vain that they ought never to have been brought before a judgment seat.
19:
One Greek word decides how insulting the sentence is, and four of them defend the governor. Barnes gives two reasons for taking it in a good sense: it was the word for the worship of the Greeks and Romans, and so of Festus himself; and he knew Agrippa was a Jew. Clarke puts it as a question: is it likely a mere procurator would so speak to a king about his own religion, which he could not do without offering the highest insult? Ellicott says the term is comparatively neutral, one an outsider might use of any local religion he did not accept; Robertson concedes it with a reservation, that Festus would hardly mean superstition, whatever he thought, because Agrippa was a Jew. Gill alone lets the harder rendering stand, and lists the questions: the law Paul was said to have spoken against, the temple he was said to have polluted, the resurrection.

On the next phrase they abandon all charity. Robertson calls ‘one Jesus’ the climax of supercilious scorn toward Paul and his Master alike, and then makes the finest observation here: with all his top-loftical airs, Festus has correctly stated the centre of Paul’s preaching, Jesus as no longer dead but living. Barnes says it shows how a Roman magistrate could speak of the glorious truth of the Christian religion. Clarke turns it on the reader: in this way does this poor heathen speak of the death and resurrection of Christ, and many who profess Christianity appear no farther enlightened. Wesley addresses the governor: how coldly he mentions the things of last importance, and thus does he speak of him to whom every knee shall bow. Why did he doubt? Only because he did not search the evidence; otherwise it might have grown into full conviction, and his illustrious prisoner have led him into the glorious liberty of the children of God.

The plea of perplexity is not quite believed. Ellicott says the word implies more than mere doubt, and that the perplexity is his justification for laying the matter before a prince who, being a Jew, might judge it better. Robertson notices this is not the reason the narrative gave earlier, a wish to curry favour with the Jews, but allows both motives could be true. Barnes will not let it stand: if Paul was guilty of no violation of the laws, he should have been discharged at once.

The imperial title interests them too. Barnes explains that the word denotes what is venerable, first applied to the emperor under whom Christ was born. Ellicott traces it outward — the name given to Samaria, the month dedicated to the first emperor, the memory kept alive in Augsburg and Sebastopol. Robertson adds the sharpest point: the term carries the notion of worship, and fell in with the tendency toward emperor-worship which Christians afterwards opposed so bitterly.

How the king came to ask is a study in character. Robertson hears courtesy in the tense, an imperfect rather than a blunt present, a compliment to the story Festus had told; Ellicott renders it, I also was myself wishing — the wish was not formed now for the first time. Calvin is severest: Agrippa so desired to hear Paul that he was ashamed to own it, lest Festus think he came for some end other than to salute him; and we may gather how cold the desire was, since he let many days pass before showing any sign of it. So the holy minister of Christ is brought forth as on a stage, that a profane man may cheer up his guest; but the matter was turned to another end by the secret providence of God, and such report went abroad as made much for the confirmation of the godly. Barnes says it from the other side: this wish gave occasion to the noblest defence ever made before any tribunal.
23:
The word for pomp is unusual, and sets them all thinking. Barnes and Clarke render it literally as phantasy, a show or parade; Robertson notes it is the only instance of the noun in the New Testament. Wesley adds only that the company was the chief officers, military and civil. Then Clarke and Ellicott make the same observation independently, the sharpest thing in the chapter: these children of Herod the Great made their pompous appearance in the very city where, a few years before, their father had been smitten for his pride and eaten of worms. Clarke draws the moral: how seldom do the living lay any of God’s judgments to heart. Ellicott finds an almost tragic pathos in it — the vice was inherited, the lesson had not been learnt.

What kind of proceeding this was they define carefully. Clarke insists it was not a trial: no Jews were present to accuse him, and he could not be tried anywhere but at Rome, having appealed. Robertson calls the hearing semi-official, names the room as the place set aside for hearing causes, and thinks the detail shows the historian was present. Ellicott adds that this was the first fulfilment of the promise that Paul should bear witness before kings. Calvin takes it further. Agrippa and his sister do not come like humble disciples, but bring such pomp as may stop their ears and blind their eyes, so it is no marvel they were not brought to obey Christ; yet the pomp is recorded so we may know that in a great assembly Paul had leave not merely to plead as a defendant but to preach. He comes forth as a teacher, so that the truth of God broke out of his bands, spread abroad with a free course, and came even unto us.

Chrysostom reads the speech as an acquittal delivered by the wrong man. See what an audience is gathered for Paul, he says; and Paul brought forth is proclaimed conqueror, for Festus himself acquits him. Mark how he accuses them while he acquits him — what an abundance of justifications! After all these examinations the judge finds no way to condemn him, and that he had nothing to say is itself a proof of Paul’s spotlessness. Robertson reaches the same verdict by grammar: all the charges slipped away or were tripped up, and Festus, confessing he had nothing left, convicts himself of gross insincerity — by his own statement he should have set Paul free. Gill puts it plainly — nothing but a heap of confused notions.

The phrase ‘my lord’ detains four of them. Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott report that the first two emperors refused the title as abominable, one saying he was lord only of his slaves, and that later emperors, Nero among them, were glad of it. Robertson makes the largest observation here. The same word was claimed by the Christians for Christ, and became the test in the Roman persecutions, when a martyr steadily refused to say Lord Caesar and insisted on Lord Jesus though it meant certain death; and Paul had this in mind in writing that no one can say Jesus is Lord except in the Holy Spirit.

Why Festus staged it is guessed at rather than known. Calvin offers two possibilities: that he hoped to coax Paul into letting the appeal fall, or that he went subtly to work to learn what the king and chief men thought, so as to shift the blame if the prisoner went free. To whatever end, Calvin adds, he condemns himself by his own mouth. Clarke ends with a use: it is lawful to avail ourselves, even in God’s cause, of the civil privileges his mercy has given us, for it is often better to fall into the hands of the heathen than of men whose hearts a mistaken religion has filled with persecuting zeal.
